label: Coordinates
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 107 to 134 and treats coordinates as a translation device between synthetic geometry and computable invariants. We move from a point on a line, through Cartesian and polar descriptions of the plane, to conics, triangle coordinates, and finally three-dimensional surfaces, asking always what each equation makes visible.

label: Cartesian and Polar
notes: Descartes addresses each point by an ordered pair against perpendicular axes, while polar coordinates name the same point by distance and direction from a pole. Neither language is superior; we choose Cartesian for lines and rectangles, polar for circles and spirals, and translate freely between them as the geometry demands.

label: The Equation of a Line
notes: A straight line becomes a first-degree equation in two variables, and the distance and angle formulas follow from the inner product. The distance between two points is a square root of squared coordinate differences, while the angle between two lines is fixed by the ratio of their direction numbers.

label: Conics by Focus and Directrix
notes: Each conic is the locus of points whose distance to a fixed focus is a constant multiple of the distance to a fixed directrix. That constant is the eccentricity. Below one, the curve closes into an ellipse; equal to one, it is a parabola; above one, it opens into a hyperbola.

label: Conics as Plane Sections
notes: Apollonius saw the three conics as sections of one cone cut at increasing tilt. A horizontal cut gives a circle, a gentle tilt an ellipse, a cut parallel to a slant edge a parabola, and a steeper cut both branches of a hyperbola. The eccentricity records the tilt angle of the cutting plane.

label: Standard Conic Equations
notes: In axis-aligned coordinates the ellipse and hyperbola become sums and differences of squared ratios equal to one, while the parabola is purely quadratic in a single variable. The foci sit along the major axis, and the semi-axes and the focal distance obey a simple Pythagorean relation that ties eccentricity to shape.

label: The General Second Degree
notes: Every conic is captured by one general second-degree equation in two variables. The discriminant of its quadratic part classifies the curve: negative gives an ellipse, zero a parabola, positive a hyperbola. Rotating the axes removes the cross term, exposing the principal directions and the true shape behind any tilted equation.

label: Barycentric Coordinates
notes: Mobius weights the three vertices of a triangle so that a point is their balance point, or centroid of the loaded masses. Only the ratios of the weights matter, so the coordinates are homogeneous. A point lies inside the triangle exactly when all three weights can be taken positive, giving an intuitive area picture.

label: Areal Coordinates
notes: Normalizing the barycentric weights to sum to one turns them into the three signed areas of the subtriangles formed by the point and the edges, divided by the whole area. Each areal coordinate is literally the fraction of the triangle subtended from the opposite side, so the coordinates read off as proportions.

label: Trilinear Coordinates and Centers
notes: Trilinear coordinates measure a point by its signed perpendicular distances to the three sides. Classical centers acquire memorable forms: the incenter is one to one to one, the centroid uses the reciprocals of the sides, and the circumcenter and orthocenter follow from cosines. Symmetry in the labels signals a genuine triangle center.

label: Circular and Hyperbolic Functions
notes: The unit circle parameterized by cosine and sine satisfies x squared plus y squared equals one, while the rectangular hyperbola parameterized by hyperbolic cosine and sine satisfies x squared minus y squared equals one. The analogy is exact apart from a sign in the metric, and the sector area plays the role of the parameter.

label: The Equiangular Spiral
notes: The logarithmic spiral has polar equation r equals a times e to the b theta, so rotating the angle multiplies the radius by a fixed factor and reproduces the same shape at a new scale. Its tangent meets every radius at one constant angle, a genuine invariant that makes it the curve unchanged by spiral similarity.

label: Coordinates in Space
notes: In three dimensions a line is parametric, a plane is one linear equation, a sphere is one quadratic equation, and a tangent plane is read from the gradient. Quadric surfaces include the ruled hyperbolic paraboloid, whose two families of straight lines sweep a curved surface, showing how compact equations encode rich spatial structure.

label: Synthesis
notes: Coordinates compress a geometric decision into a computable invariant: a discriminant classifies a conic, a triangle of weights locates a center, and a single equation pins a surface. Each representation is chosen because it makes a different invariant easy to inspect, and a second representation always checks the first against error.
